One night, when she was only eight, the situation escalated to a point that still haunted her. She remembered the darkness of her room, the way it seemed to close in on her as she lay awake, listening to the chaos unfold. The sound of her mother’s terrified cries and the heavy thud of a body hitting the floor sent her heart racing with an urgency she could not escape. It was a moment that had crystallized in her mind, vivid and unrelenting, as if it were happening all over again whenever she found herself in dark, enclosed spaces. Now, as a train conductor, Camila faced the eerie silence of the tunnels, which were often punctuated by the sudden screech of metal on metal or the unexpected rumble of machinery. These loud noises would catapult her back to those nights of fear, her heart pounding as she felt a familiar wave of panic wash over her. Each time the train entered a dimly lit tunnel, her body would tense, and she would find herself checking her surroundings, her mind racing with thoughts of safety. Yet, this strategy only served to amplify her anxiety, leading her to neglect her own needs, including food. She often found herself undereating, convinced that if she could just stay busy enough, the haunting memories would fade.
